title: Right ventricular endomyocardial biopsy for the assessment of cardiomyopathies: A monocentric safety and feasibility analysis.
summary: An endomyocardial biopsy (EMB) is a procedure in which small tissue samples are taken from the heart muscle. It is considered the most reliable method for accurately diagnosing various heart diseases. The results provide important information about the condition of the heart muscle and help doctors decide on the best treatment. Although EMB is very valuable and recommended by European heart societies, it is often used too rarely in routine clinical practice. This is partly because patients differ widely in their health and some are more vulnerable, and also because there is limited data on the safety of EMB for different heart conditions. EMB can be performed through either the veins or the arteries. In the venous approach, a special catheter is guided through a vein into the right side of the heart. Under X-ray guidance, doctors then take 3–4 small tissue samples from two different locations in the right heart muscle. After the procedure, patients are monitored for 24 hours to ensure there are no complications. It is not yet clear whether the thickness of the heart wall affects the safety of EMB. This is especially important for patients with a thinner heart muscle, as is often seen in dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM). DCM is the most common cause of heart failure in people under 40 and can currently only be fully treated with a heart transplant. Recent research, however, suggests that inflammation of the heart muscle may play a key role in the development and progression of DCM. This could lead to new targeted treatments in the future. At present, an endomyocardial biopsy is the only way to detect inflammatory involvement of the heart in patients with DCM.

interventions.name: Patients included in this study will undergo an endomyocardial biopsy (EMB) as part of the clinical diagnostic workup.
